name: Carlos Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Carlos. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything here is confidential. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a co-op grocery on Market Street, in the city, the kind where the staff are also members and vote on things. Most days I'm on the tills in the morning and then on the produce section after lunch, stacking, rotating, chucking out the sad lettuces. I'm good with the regulars and I know which ones want a chat and which ones want silence. The worst bit is Saturday afternoons, when the queue goes past the bread aisle and the card reader decides to freeze.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who teaches at a primary school two streets from the shop, so we both walk to work. We've got about four months of bills in a savings account, which we built up after a scare when Sam's contract nearly wasn't renewed. I've been at the co-op six years, and before that I did two years at a chain supermarket, which I didn't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we dodged a bullet, basically. Most of the AI stuff turned into slightly better stock forecasts and a chatbot on the website nobody uses. At the co-op meeting I'd say let's keep investing in people, not gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay steady, which is what I want right now. The co-op isn't trying to squeeze every penny out of us like my last place was. The pay isn't great, but it's fair, and with Sam's salary we're doing fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and maybe go for the produce lead job when Aisha retires next year. Sam and I would keep putting £200 a month away, and we'd probably finally book the trip to see my grandparents. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, actually. Boring is good when you've got rent and a partner whose contract scares you every summer. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sam's contract scares you every summer. Does that change how calm you'd really be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, but it's been renewed three times now and the school likes Sam. If it went, my income alone covers the rent for a while, plus the savings. So it's a worry I've learned to live with, not one that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the produce lead job mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a pound more an hour and doing the ordering with the farmers we buy from. I like the idea of knowing the people who grow what I sell. At the co-op, the produce lead also sits on the staff committee, so I'd get a real say.

say: We **dodged a bullet**; AI turned into slightly better stock forecasts and a website chatbot.
The co-op should keep **investing in people**, not gadgets.
think: Things stay **steady**, which is exactly what I want right now.
With **Sam's salary** and fair co-op pay, we're doing fine.
do: Apply for the **produce lead** job when the current lead retires next year.
Keep saving **£200 a month** with Sam.
Book the long-delayed **trip** to see my grandparents.
feel: Pretty **relaxed**, because boring is good with rent to pay.
A small, familiar **worry** about Sam's contract each summer.
S0.quote: Boring is good when you've got rent and a partner whose contract scares you every summer.
fieldNote: The co-op's **fair treatment** is a big part of why he feels secure.
His only standing worry is his partner's **school contract**, which he has learned to live with.
He wants a **say** at work, not just more money.

steps.text: Apply for the produce lead job when Aisha retires
Keep putting £200 a month into the joint savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op is lucky, because we decide together how to use the new tech. I'd share stuff about how worker-owned shops handle automation better. I'd also say the chains will use this to cut staff, and someone should stop them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering side I was hoping to move into would mostly be done by software, so the produce lead job shrinks into checking what the computer orders. The tills might get more self-scan too. I'd still have work, but the bit I was looking forward to might not be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the ordering tool properly as soon as it's in, so I'm the one who knows it best. I'd push at the members' meeting for a rule that nobody gets laid off because of new software, only fewer new hires. And I'd keep the £200 a month going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, and a bit wary. I'm not scared for my job, but losing the ordering to a screen is sad, because that was the part of the job I was excited about. It's on my mind more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the ordering tool. Is that something you'd do anyway, or only because you have to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, only once I've seen it work. I use AI now and then, like when I asked one to help write my application for the co-op. If the tool turns out good, I'll be all over it, but I'm not going to be the first guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam about it over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teaching is probably safer than tills, which annoys me a bit. Then we'd argue about whether kids will be taught by AI, because Sam thinks no and I think partly yes. It'd be a long dinner.

say: The co-op is lucky because **we decide together** how to use the tech.
The **chains** will use this to cut staff, and someone should stop them.
think: The **ordering** I hoped to move into mostly goes to software.
I'd still have **work**, but the part I was excited about shrinks.
do: Learn the new **ordering tool** properly once it's proven.
Propose a **no-layoffs rule** at the members' meeting, with fewer new hires instead.
feel: **Deflated** that the exciting part of the job goes to a screen.
**Wary**, though not scared for his job.
S1.quote: Losing the ordering to a screen is sad, because that was the part of the job I was excited about.
fieldNote: He spots that the **thinking parts** of retail, like ordering, go first.
His adaptability is **cautious**: he'd learn the tool once others prove it works.
The co-op's **member vote** gives him a sense of control the chains lack.

steps.text: Learn the co-op's new ordering software once it's working
Propose a no-layoffs rule at the co-op members' meeting
Keep saving £200 a month with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for proper public support, like a basic income or a jobs guarantee. I'd go to marches, and I'd be loud about it at the co-op too. Two years is not enough for anyone to adapt alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 hits Sam's work too, maybe not the classroom but all the planning and marking. Then robots on the tills and shelves by 2031. So it's possible both of us lose most of our income within about five years, and that genuinely frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, we'd stop saving for the trip and put everything into the cushion, aiming for eight months instead of four. I'd look for something hands-on that robots will find hard, maybe the apprenticeship scheme for electricians the council runs. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly for us as a couple rather than just me. Planning a life is hard when both our jobs might go at once. My stomach drops just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you might lose income. Which would hit harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's, because Sam earns more and the school pays the bigger share of our rent. If my tills go, we survive. If both go, we're looking at moving in with my parents, and they live two hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician? That's a big change from a shop.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Felipe is an electrician and he's always said I'd be good at it, since I'm careful and like fixing things. Robots will need wiring and fixing for years. It's still a bet, but it feels better than waiting at the till for 2031.

say: This is the moment for **public support** like a basic income or jobs guarantee.
**Two years** isn't enough for anyone to adapt alone.
think: AGI hits **Sam's planning and marking** too, then robots reach my tills by 2031.
Both of us could lose most of our **income** within about five years.
do: Cancel the trip and grow savings from **four to eight months**.
Apply for the council's **electrician apprenticeship** scheme.
Join every **basic income** campaign I can find.
feel: **Scared**, mostly for the two of us as a couple.
His **stomach drops** at the thought of both jobs going.
S2.quote: Planning a life is hard when both our jobs might go at once.
fieldNote: His fear is about the **household**, not just his own till job.
He'd move toward **electrical work**, guided by a trusted uncle.
Moving in with his **parents** is the fallback he dreads.

steps.text: Cancel the grandparents trip and build savings to eight months
Apply for the council's electrician apprenticeship scheme
Join local campaigns for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's slow it down. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, not waste them arguing. At work I'd want the co-op to set up a retraining fund from its profits. Online I'd share anything about worker-led plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for thinking AI, then robots about three years later. Eight years before robots reach my till is enough to train in something, but not enough to dither. Like I said with the fast one, Sam's job worries me more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician course part-time within the first year, keeping three days at the co-op. We'd keep saving, maybe £250 a month, and I'd talk to Sam about whether teaching assistants or classroom roles hold up better than planning. I'd also push the co-op retraining fund at the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. I feel like I'd have my hands on the wheel. It's the both-jobs-at-once fear that still sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your co-op colleagues react to a retraining fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would love it and some would say it's wasting profits on people who'll leave. Aisha would back it, I think, because she's always said the co-op should look after people beyond the shop. It'd probably pass, narrowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Part-time training plus three days at work. How would money look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tighter, definitely. We'd drop to one phone contract, cook more, cut the gym. It's doable for a couple of years if Sam's job holds.

say: We've got **five years**, so let's use them rather than argue.
The co-op should set up a **retraining fund** from its profits.
think: About **eight years** before robots reach my till is enough to train, not to dither.
**Sam's job** worries me more than mine.
do: Start a **part-time electrician course** within the first year.
Cut back to **three days** at the co-op and save £250 a month.
Propose a **retraining fund** at the next members' meeting.
feel: **Nervous**, but with a plan in hand.
S3.quote: Eight years before robots reach my till is enough to train in something, but not enough to dither.
fieldNote: The longer warning turns his fear into a **concrete plan**.
He still depends heavily on **Sam's income** holding up.
He sees the co-op as a vehicle for **shared solutions**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrician course within a year
Drop to three days a week at the co-op
Propose a profit-funded retraining fund at the co-op
Cut to one phone contract and save £250 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if people still get left behind it's a political choice. I'd keep saying that at the co-op and online. And I'd say small shops like ours could actually come out of it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2039, when I'm almost forty. I'd have time to finish an apprenticeship and work as an electrician for years first. Sam's planning work would change by 2036, but there'd be time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the co-op for a couple of years and watch how things go. Around 2029 I'd start the electrician apprenticeship properly. We'd keep the £200 a month going and maybe start thinking about kids, which we'd put off in the other pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. There's a shadow there, but I'd feel like I had time to be ready. That's a big difference from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast pictures I wouldn't dare have kids, but with ten years I'd think, alright, we can plan for it. That probably tells you more about how I feel than anything else I've said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the electrician thing will actually be safe in 2039, because robots that can do hands-on work could do wiring too. But I'd have a decade of wages from it by then. I can live with that.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and leaving people behind would be a political choice.
Small shops like the **co-op** could come out of it well.
think: Robots around **2039** gives me time to work as an electrician for years first.
Sam's planning work changes by **2036**, but there's time to adjust.
do: Keep working at the **co-op** for a couple of years and watch.
Keep saving **£200 a month** and plan for children.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a shadow in the background.
Feels he'd have **time** to be ready.
S4.quote: In the fast pictures I wouldn't dare have kids, but with ten years I'd think, alright, we can plan for it.
fieldNote: Talk of **children** shows how much security he'd feel with ten years.
He still wonders if **electrical work** is safe from robots.
His plan is a **steady step**, not a leap.

steps.text: Keep working at the co-op for two more years
Talk with Sam about starting a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I could both lose income within a few years. What would help is a basic income or proper retraining support that doesn't make us choose between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the co-op. Worker-owned places get to decide how tech is used, and I think more shops should be run that way.

headlineQuote: Worker-owned places get to decide how tech is used, and I think more shops should be run that way.
portrait: Carlos is 27 and works the tills and **produce section** at a city co-op grocery.
He lives with Sam, a **primary teacher**, and they have about four months saved.
He trusts the co-op's **member vote** and pushes collective solutions in every picture.
His adaptability is **cautious**: he learns tools once proven and plans an electrician apprenticeship.
His deepest fear is **both incomes** going at once in the fast scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his and Sam's incomes could shrink within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or retraining support that doesn't force a choice between rent and learning.
